text: Louis Moreau Gottschalk (May 8, 1829 – December 18, 1869) was an American composer, pianist, and virtuoso performer of his own romantic piano works. Born in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Edward Gottschalk and Aimée Marie Bruslé, he had six siblings, five of whom were half-siblings by his father's biracial mistress. The family lived in a cottage at Royal and Esplanade in the Vieux Carré and later moved to 518 Conti Street, where his maternal grandmother Bruslé and nurse Sally, both Saint Dominican Creoles, influenced his exposure to diverse musical traditions. He began playing the piano early and made his informal public debut in 1840 at the St. Charles Hotel. At age 13, he left the United States for Europe to pursue classical training, but the Paris Conservatoire rejected his application without hearing him, with head of the piano faculty Pierre Zimmerman stating, "America is a country of steam engines." Despite this, he gained recognition through family connections. Compositions such as Bamboula (Danse Des Nègres) and La Savane established him as an authentic American composer, incorporating African musical traditions and serving as precursors to jazz; they are considered the first examples of Louisiana Creole music in classical culture. After a concert at the Salle Pleyel, Chopin praised him, saying, "Give me your hand, my child; I predict that you will become the king of pianists," and both Franz Liszt and Charles-Valentin Alkan acknowledged his exceptional talent. Returning to the United States in 1853, he traveled widely, including a sojourn in Cuba in 1854, which led to a series of trips to Central and South America. He visited Puerto Rico after his Havana debut and composed Souvenir de Porto Rico; Marche des gibaros, Op. 31 (RO250), probably in 1857, a march based on a Puerto Rican folk song form, with "gibaros" referring to the jíbaros or Puerto Rican peasantry. After his tour, he rested in New Jersey before returning to New York City, where he took on the young Venezuelan student Teresa Carreño, an exception to his skepticism about prodigies. Though he gave her only a few lessons, she remembered him fondly and performed his music throughout her life; she later performed for Abraham Lincoln and became a renowned pianist known as the "Valkyrie of the Piano." In late 1855 and early 1856, he connected with notable figures in the New York art world, including sculptor Erastus Dow Palmer, composer George William Warren, and landscape painter Frederic Edwin Church, who had also traveled in Latin America and produced large-scale paintings of South American subjects. Gottschalk dedicated a Mazurka poétique to Church, who gave him a small, now-unidentified landscape painting; he also possibly collaborated with Warren on The Andes, Marche di Bravoura, inspired by Church’s painting The Heart of the Andes. By the 1860s, he was the best-known pianist in the New World, though he only returned to New Orleans occasionally, always introducing himself as a native. He composed the tarantella, Grande Tarantelle, Op. 67, subtitled Célèbre Tarentelle, between 1858 and 1864. In May 1865, a San Francisco newspaper reported that he had traveled 95,000 miles by rail and given 1,000 concerts. Later that year, he was forced to leave the United States due to an alleged affair with a student at the Oakland Female Seminary in Oakland, California; he denied wrongdoing, claiming the incident was a smear campaign by a rival of the piano manufacturer Chickering & Sons, the brand he used for his tours. He never returned to the United States and instead traveled to South America, where he continued performing. On November 24, 1869, at the Teatro Lyrico Fluminense in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, he collapsed from yellow fever after finishing the piece Morte! (Death) and just as he began playing Tremolo. He never recovered. He died on December 18, 1869, at age 40, at his hotel in Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, likely from an overdose of quinine, with an essay by Jeremy Nicholas noting that he died of empyema due to a ruptured abdominal abscess. In 1870, his remains were returned to the United States and buried at Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn, New York City. His original burial site was marked by a marble monument with an "Angel of Music" statue, which was damaged by vandals in 1959. In October 2012, after nearly 15 years of fundraising, a new "Angel of Music" statue, created by Giancarlo Biagi and Jill Burkee, was unveiled. Gottschalk's music was popular during his lifetime, with early works like Bamboula, La Savane, Le Bananier, and Le Mancenillier based on his childhood memories in Louisiana and regarded as the earliest pieces of creole music in classical culture. His 13-minute opera Escenas campestres retains value, and the Bamboula theme appears in his Symphony No. 1: A Night in the Tropics. A melody from Souvenirs d'Andalousie forms the basis of Ernesto Lecuona’s popular 20th-century piece "Malagueña." Many of his compositions were lost or destroyed after his death. Richard Jackson edited a 1973 collection of his piano music and organized an exhibition at the New York Public Library. Vanguard Records released the first important recordings of his orchestral works, including A Night in the Tropics, by Maurice Abravanel and the Utah Symphony Orchestra. Vox Records issued a multi-disc collection, later reissued on CD, including world premiere recordings of the original orchestrations conducted by Igor Buketoff and Samuel Adler. In 1984, Nimbus Records released The Lady Fainted, a selection of piano fantasies, caprices, meditations, and paraphrases performed by Alan Marks. Lambert Orkis recorded a selection of his music on an 1865 Chickering concert grand in 1988 as part of The Smithsonian Collection of Recordings. Gottschalk’s music was used in the soundtrack for the Michel Deville film Aux Petits Bonheurs, played by Noël Lee on a Steinway piano and released by Erato Records in 1994. Beginning in the 1990s, Philip Martin recorded most of Gottschalk’s extant piano music for Hyperion Records. Howard Breslin wrote a historical novel about him, Concert Grand, in 1963. A version of Bamboula with added lyrics was recorded in April 1934 by Abel Beauregard’s dance band, the Orchestre Créole Matou from Guadeloupe, marking the first recording of the composition; the first classical piano recordings of his works were not made until 1956 by Eugene List. Other recordings of the bamboula rhythm heard in New Orleans’ Congo Square, such as the 1950 Haitian voodoo recording Baboule Dance (three drums), the 1962 Cuban folk tune Rezos Congos (Bamboula, Conga Music), and Dr. John’s 1970s recording of Litanie des Saints from Goin' Back to New Orleans, are linked to Gottschalk’s work. Comments by musicologist Bruno Blum are included in each of these releases.
